chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Abu Ishaq al-Kaffaf, from Muhammad ibn Abi Zayd, from Abu Harun al-Makfuf, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Would it please you if you had a guide, O Abu Harun?' I said, 'Yes, may I be sacrificed for you.' So he gave me thirty dinars and said: 'Buy a Kasoumiyya servant.' So I bought him. When I went to Hajj, I visited him. He said to him: 'How do you find your guide, O Abu Harun?' He said, 'Good.' So he gave him twenty-five dinars and said to him: 'Buy a Shamiyya slave girl, for their children are a delight.' So I bought a Shamiyya slave girl and married her to him. She bore me three daughters. I gifted one of them to one of the children of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), and I hope that He will make my reward from it Paradise. And two daughters remained, which brought me thousands of pleasures.

key_terms.كُسُومِيّاً: From Kasum (a region, likely in the Caucasus)

ai.seo_question: How did the Imams manage slaves and their offspring in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: This narrative from Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) illustrates the practical management of slaves as economic assets within the family structure, specifically highlighting the strategy of breeding for lineage and utility. The Imam guides the companion Abu Harun to first purchase a male servant as a guide, and then a female slave to bear children, demonstrating how slave ownership was integrated into daily life and family expansion. This practice underscores the Shia legal perspective on 'mukataba' and the social utility of domestic slaves, where offspring could enhance the master's household status and provide potential means for manumission.
